placeholders.name: SOURCE: Annual Report 2025
placeholders.what: This is the label for your first source document — replace "Annual Report 2025" with the real name and date/year of whatever document you're pasting first. Keep the word "SOURCE:" so the AI knows this line marks a new document starting, and use a name specific enough that you'd recognize it in a list of ten documents six months from now.
examples: SOURCE: Annual Report 2025
SOURCE: Client Website – About Us page, accessed Jan 2026
SOURCE: Board Meeting Minutes, Nov 12 2025

placeholders.name: PASTE TEXT
placeholders.what: Paste the actual text of that source document here — not a summary of it, the real content (copy from the PDF, the deck, the memo, or the webpage). The more complete the paste, the more the briefing can actually cite from it instead of guessing at what the document says.
examples: Revenue for FY2025 was $42.3M, up 11% from FY2024. Gross margin held steady at 38%. The board approved a new regional expansion into the Midwest, expected to launch Q3 2026. Headcount grew from 210 to 248 employees.

The client's stated top priority for this engagement is reducing customer churn, currently running at 14% annually, which leadership considers unsustainable given their growth targets. A secondary goal is streamlining the onboarding process, which currently takes an average of 19 days.

Prior consultant (2024) recommended a phased rollout of a new CRM system, estimated at 6 months and $180K. Client leadership deferred this recommendation citing budget constraints, but flagged it as a 2026 priority in the closing memo.

placeholders.name: SOURCE: Prior Consulting Deck 2024
placeholders.what: The label for your second source document, following the same [SOURCE: name] format as the first one. Use whatever this document actually is — a prior firm's deck, an internal strategy memo, a set of board minutes — with enough detail in the name to tell it apart from your other sources.
examples: SOURCE: Prior Consulting Deck 2024
SOURCE: Internal Strategy Memo, Q4 2025
SOURCE: Competitor Analysis Deck, McKinsey engagement 2023

placeholders.name: SOURCE: Kickoff Memo
placeholders.what: The label for your third source document — commonly the internal memo your own team or the client wrote ahead of the kickoff call, laying out what the engagement is supposed to cover. Add as many additional [SOURCE: name] / [PASTE TEXT] pairs as you need beyond the three shown if you have more documents.
examples: SOURCE: Kickoff Memo
SOURCE: Engagement Kickoff Memo, prepared by client CFO
SOURCE: Internal Scoping Notes from Partner Call, Jan 5 2026

placeholders.name: SOURCE
placeholders.what: You don't type anything here yourself — this is part of the instructions telling the AI how to tag every fact in the briefing (for example, a fact should be tagged [Annual Report 2025] rather than left untagged). It's shown in brackets in the prompt so the AI reproduces that exact tagging format in its answer.
examples: [Annual Report 2025]
[Kickoff Memo]
[Prior Consulting Deck 2024]

variations.label: Single-document quick briefing
variations.whenToUse: You only have one document so far (say, just the annual report) and want a fast first-pass briefing rather than waiting to gather every source before the kickoff call.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me build a briefing document from one client source before an engagement kickoff. Use ONLY information contained in the source below — do not add outside knowledge about the company or industry, and do not infer anything the document doesn't actually state.

[SOURCE: NAME AND DATE OF THE DOCUMENT]
[PASTE TEXT]

Produce a briefing with these sections:
1. Company overview (2-3 sentences)
2. Key facts and figures (bullet list)
3. Stated priorities / goals, if mentioned
4. Gaps this single document leaves — what I still don't know that I'll need before the kickoff call

Do not state anything as fact unless it's actually in the source text above.

variations.label: Claude Project version for an ongoing engagement
variations.whenToUse: You're setting this up as a Claude Project rather than a single chat, so every future conversation in this engagement can reference the same verified sources without re-pasting them.
variations.prompt: Create a new Claude Project for this engagement. Upload each client document to the project's knowledge, labeled clearly with its name and date. Then, in a new chat within the project, ask: "Using only the documents in this project's knowledge, build a briefing with these sections: company overview, key facts and figures, stated priorities/goals, prior initiatives, and open questions for the kickoff meeting. Tag every claim with its source document. Do not combine facts from two documents into a new claim unless you clearly label it as an inference and name both sources. If sources disagree on a fact, list it as a contradiction instead of picking one."

variations.label: Mid-engagement update briefing
variations.whenToUse: You already built an initial briefing weeks ago and now have new documents (updated financials, a new stakeholder memo) — you want an updated briefing that shows what changed, not a briefing built from scratch.
variations.prompt:
I previously built a briefing from earlier client sources. Here is that original briefing:
[PASTE YOUR EXISTING BRIEFING]

Here are new sources I've received since then:
[SOURCE: NAME AND DATE]
[PASTE TEXT]

Update the briefing using ONLY the original briefing plus the new source(s) above. Specifically:
1. Flag any fact in the new source that contradicts or updates something in the original briefing.
2. Add any genuinely new key facts, priorities, or initiatives, tagged with the new source.
3. Do not remove or silently alter anything from the original briefing — mark changes explicitly as "UPDATED" rather than deleting the old version.

followUps.label: Verify a specific claim against the source
followUps.prompt: For the fact you listed under "[Kickoff Memo]" about their stated priorities, quote the exact sentence from that source that supports it, word for word. If you can't find an exact supporting sentence, say so instead of paraphrasing something close to it.

followUps.label: Add a list of documents I'm missing
followUps.prompt: Based on the gaps and open questions you flagged, list the specific documents or data (e.g. "most recent org chart," "last two years of churn data") that would close those gaps, so I know what to request before or during the kickoff call.

followUps.label: Resolve a flagged contradiction
followUps.prompt: You flagged a contradiction between the annual report and the prior consulting deck on headcount. Lay out both figures side by side with their exact source, and suggest two or three plausible, non-speculative reasons they might differ (e.g. different reporting periods) without picking which one is correct.

followUps.label: Compress to a one-minute verbal briefing
followUps.prompt: Condense this into five spoken sentences I could say out loud in the first minute of the kickoff call to show I've done my homework — no bullet points, just plain sentences, and keep every fact tagged so I know what I can say with confidence.

con-b1-synthesize-client-documents-brief.walkthrough:
Dana is a consultant starting a six-week engagement with a regional healthcare staffing company. The kickoff call is in ninety minutes, and Dana has three documents sitting unread: last year's annual report, a prior consultant's 2024 deck, and the internal kickoff memo her own partner wrote after the sales call.

Dana opens Claude, creates a new Project for the engagement, and uploads three sources to its knowledge: [SOURCE: Annual Report 2025] with the report's key paragraphs, [SOURCE: Prior Consulting Deck 2024] with a few slides' worth of text, and [SOURCE: Kickoff Memo] with her partner's two-paragraph summary of what the client wants.

In a chat inside the project, she pastes the briefing prompt. Claude returns a structured briefing: a two-sentence company overview tagged to the annual report, a bullet list of facts (revenue, headcount, the client's stated churn problem), a priorities section quoting the client's own words from the kickoff memo, and — importantly — a contradictions section flagging that the annual report lists 340 employees while the prior deck cites 310, a discrepancy nobody had noticed. It closes with four open questions, including whether the earlier consultant's CRM recommendation was ever revisited.

Dana sends a follow-up asking Claude to quote the exact sentence behind the churn-priority claim, just to be sure nothing was paraphrased loosely. The quote checks out. She also asks for the whole thing condensed into five spoken sentences she can say naturally to open the call.

Twenty-five minutes after starting, Dana walks into the kickoff call able to reference the headcount discrepancy directly, ask about the deferred CRM recommendation, and open with a summary that makes clear she read everything — without having actually read all forty pages herself. The verified briefing stays in the project's knowledge for the rest of the engagement, so the next chat starts from the same confirmed baseline.

placeholders.name: STATE THE DECISION/ACTION
placeholders.what: Name the single concrete thing the client needs to decide or do after reading the finished deliverable — not the topic of the engagement, the actual decision. A good version is specific enough that you could imagine the client saying yes or no to it directly.
examples: Approve a $2M investment in automating the claims-processing workflow
Decide whether to exit the underperforming Northeast retail region by end of year
Choose between three vendor finalists for the new logistics platform

placeholders.name: PASTE BULLET LIST OF FINDINGS
placeholders.what: Paste your raw findings as short, factual, unordered bullets — the things you actually found in the data or interviews, not yet grouped into any argument. Each bullet should be a specific, checkable fact, not a vague theme.
examples:
- Customer churn is 22% among accounts under $10K ARR, vs. 6% above $50K ARR
- Support ticket volume doubled in the last 2 quarters without headcount growth
- Exit interviews cite "slow response time" as the top complaint in 60% of cases
- Competitor X launched a self-serve tier 8 months ago at a lower price point
- Average time-to-first-response is 14 hours, up from 5 hours a year ago

- Warehouse A is running at 94% capacity; Warehouse B is at 61%
- Shipping costs from Warehouse A rose 18% due to a new carrier contract
- Two of the three largest customers are geographically closer to Warehouse B
- Lead time from Warehouse A averages 3.2 days; from B, 2.1 days

- Only 40% of new hires complete onboarding training within the first 30 days
- Managers report spending 6+ hours/week on manual onboarding paperwork
- Employee engagement scores are 15 points lower for hires who take longer than 60 days to onboard
- HR has no automated tracking system for onboarding completion

variations.label: When you already have a storyline hunch
variations.whenToUse: You already suspect which narrative structure fits best and mainly want the AI to stress-test that one option rather than propose alternatives from scratch.
variations.prompt:
I have a list of raw findings and a storyline structure I think fits, and I want you to pressure-test it rather than propose new ones.

The decision the client needs to make at the end: [STATE THE DECISION/ACTION]
My proposed storyline structure: [NAME THE STRUCTURE, e.g. "problem-cause-solution"]

Raw findings (factual, unordered):
[PASTE BULLET LIST OF FINDINGS]

Tasks:
1. Map every finding into a section of my proposed structure. Flag any finding that doesn't fit cleanly.
2. Tell me honestly whether this structure is the strongest fit for these findings, or whether a different structure would represent the evidence more faithfully — and why.
3. If you recommend keeping my structure, write the one-page outline (section headers plus a "so what" sentence per section). If you recommend switching, explain the alternative before outlining it.

Do not invent new findings or strengthen a finding's claim to make it fit my proposed structure.

variations.label: Team-facing version with open questions flagged
variations.whenToUse: You're building the storyline for internal team alignment before the client sees anything, and want the model to also surface where the findings are still too thin to support a strong storyline.
variations.prompt:
I have a list of raw findings from a consulting engagement. Before proposing a storyline, tell me honestly where the evidence is currently too thin to support a strong argument.

The decision the client needs to make at the end: [STATE THE DECISION/ACTION]

Raw findings (factual, unordered):
[PASTE BULLET LIST OF FINDINGS]

Tasks:
1. Flag any area where the findings are suggestive but not yet strong enough to build a confident storyline section around — name what additional data or evidence would strengthen it.
2. Propose 2 storyline structures that work with the evidence as it currently stands, not the evidence you'd want to have.
3. Recommend one, and note explicitly which sections currently rest on the strongest vs. weakest evidence.

This is for internal team discussion before anything goes to the client, so be direct about weaknesses rather than smoothing over them.

variations.label: Fast single-structure version for a routine deliverable
variations.whenToUse: The deliverable is low-stakes or highly routine (an internal update, a recurring monthly readout) and you don't need to compare multiple storyline structures — you just want one clean outline quickly.
variations.prompt:
I have a list of raw findings and need a single storyline outline quickly — no need to compare alternative structures.

The decision or takeaway this needs to land: [STATE THE DECISION/ACTION]

Raw findings (factual, unordered):
[PASTE BULLET LIST OF FINDINGS]

Propose the single storyline structure you think best fits these findings, map every finding into a section (flagging anything that doesn't fit), and write a one-page outline: section headers plus a one-sentence "so what" for each. Do not invent new findings or overstate what any finding shows.

followUps.label: Argue the opposite conclusion
followUps.prompt: Using only the same findings, build the strongest plausible case for the opposite conclusion. If you can build a genuinely convincing counter-narrative, tell me specifically which findings are doing the most work in your original storyline, since those are the ones I need stronger evidence behind.

followUps.label: Check for overstated 'so what' lines
followUps.prompt: Go back through the one-page outline and check each "so what" sentence against the findings mapped to that section. Flag any "so what" that claims more certainty or a stronger causal link than the underlying findings actually support.

followUps.label: Shorten to a 3-section version
followUps.prompt: Compress this into a 3-section version of the same storyline for a shorter meeting slot, keeping the strongest findings and the decision squarely in focus. Tell me which findings you're dropping so I can decide if any of them are too important to cut.

followUps.label: Sanity-check nothing was dropped
followUps.prompt: Go back through my original bullet list of findings one more time and confirm every single one is either mapped into a section of the outline or explicitly listed as 'doesn't fit.' List any finding that's missing from both.

con-b2-structure-deliverable-storyline.walkthrough:
Marcus is two weeks into a retail-operations engagement and has eleven solid findings from data pulls and interviews, but no clear sense of how they add up to an argument. The client's steering committee meeting is Thursday, and he needs a deck outline by tomorrow morning.

He opens a blank document and first writes the one thing the committee actually needs to decide: whether to consolidate two regional warehouses into one. Then he lists his eleven findings as plain bullets — capacity numbers, shipping cost changes, customer proximity data, lead times — without trying to organize them yet.

He pastes both into the storyline prompt in Claude. The response proposes three structures: problem-cause-solution, situation-complication-resolution, and a straight cost-benefit comparison. For each, it maps his eleven findings into sections, and flags one finding — a minor note about a software licensing renewal — as not fitting cleanly anywhere. It recommends situation-complication-resolution, arguing the findings tell a clear before/after story rather than a single-cause narrative, and delivers a one-page outline with six section headers and a one-sentence so-what for each.

Marcus isn't fully convinced the recommended structure is the strongest read, so he sends a follow-up asking Claude to argue the opposite conclusion — keep both warehouses open — using the same findings. The counter-argument turns out to lean heavily on the lead-time difference, which makes Marcus realize that finding needs a second data pull to confirm before Thursday, rather than being restated confidently in a slide title.

Total time: about twenty minutes, plus a same-day request to his analyst to double-check the lead-time numbers before he finalizes the outline.

placeholders.name: INDUSTRY
placeholders.what: Name the specific industry your prospective client operates in — the more specific, the sharper the research. "Retail" is too broad to produce useful trends; "mid-size regional grocery retail" gives Gemini's Deep Research something concrete to search against.
examples: regional grocery retail
commercial property insurance
B2B SaaS for healthcare scheduling

placeholders.name: GEOGRAPHY/MARKET
placeholders.what: State the geography or market the client actually competes in — national, a specific region, or a country — since trends and competitors differ a lot by geography and a generic national answer can mislead a locally-focused client.
examples: US Midwest
UK and Ireland
Southeast Asia, primarily Singapore and Malaysia

placeholders.name: COMPANY SIZE/TYPE
placeholders.what: Describe the scale and type of company you want competitors compared against — a regional player, an enterprise chain, a specific revenue band — so the competitor list is actually relevant to your client's size rather than dominated by market leaders who aren't real comparables.
examples: regional chains with 20-80 locations
mid-market companies with $50M-$200M revenue
venture-backed startups under 100 employees

placeholders.name: SPECIFIC ANGLE, e.g. "supply chain" or "customer acquisition costs"
placeholders.what: Name the specific business function or issue the proposal needs to speak to — this is what keeps the research tightly relevant to your pitch instead of a broad industry overview that touches everything and lands nothing.
examples: supply chain resilience
customer acquisition costs
regulatory compliance costs

variations.label: Fast single-question version
variations.whenToUse: You need one sharp, sourced fact quickly — for example to open a cold email — rather than a full Deep Research report. Ask this in a regular Gemini chat with web search rather than launching a full Deep Research run, which is built for broader multi-source briefs.
variations.prompt: Give me the single most significant, current (last 12 months) trend or pressure affecting [COMPANY SIZE/TYPE] companies in the [INDUSTRY] industry in [GEOGRAPHY/MARKET], specifically related to [SPECIFIC ANGLE]. Cite the source and its publish date. If you're not highly confident in this being the single most significant trend, say so and give me the runner-up as well.

variations.label: Competitor-deep-dive version
variations.whenToUse: The proposal hinges specifically on how the client compares to two or three named competitors, not the industry broadly, and you need a focused comparison rather than general trends.
variations.prompt:
I'm preparing a proposal for a client in the [INDUSTRY] industry, [GEOGRAPHY/MARKET] market, competing directly with: [NAME 2-3 COMPETITORS].

For each competitor, with a cited source and date:
1. Their current positioning or main value proposition
2. Any recent (last 12 months) strategic move — a launch, pricing change, expansion, or public statement
3. Anything publicly known about their performance or market share trend

Then summarize in 2-3 sentences what a client competing against all of them would need to differentiate on. Flag any competitor where you couldn't find recent, reliable information rather than filling the gap with speculation.

variations.label: Slide-ready summary version
variations.whenToUse: You've already run the initial research and verified the sources, and now want the confirmed points reformatted into short, proposal-ready sentences instead of a research writeup.
variations.prompt:
Using only the following verified research points, write 3-4 short, proposal-ready sentences I can drop into the "why now" section of a client proposal. Each sentence should state one trend or fact plainly, in a confident but not salesy tone, without a citation in the sentence itself (I'll keep citations in my own backup notes).

Verified points:
[PASTE YOUR CONFIRMED RESEARCH POINTS, WITH SOURCES, FROM THE EARLIER RESEARCH STEP]

followUps.label: Narrow to the client's exact size and region
followUps.prompt: That's still broader than my client's actual situation. Narrow this specifically to [COMPANY SIZE/TYPE] companies in [GEOGRAPHY/MARKET] — if the data doesn't exist at that specific scope, tell me clearly rather than presenting the broader answer as if it applies directly.

followUps.label: Push back on a confident-sounding figure
followUps.prompt: You stated [SPECIFIC FIGURE OR CLAIM] with what sounds like high confidence. Open the actual source and quote the exact sentence that supports this figure, and tell me if the source itself expresses any uncertainty about it.

followUps.label: Turn findings into proposal-ready language
followUps.prompt: Turn the verified findings above into 3 short sentences I can use in the proposal's opening section, written plainly and confidently, without citation markers in the sentence text.

followUps.label: Flag anything that's now out of date
followUps.prompt: Review the sources you cited and flag any that are older than 12 months, or where a more recent source might have superseded the trend or figure. I'd rather cut a stale point than use it.

con-i1-industry-research-before-proposal.walkthrough:
Priya is putting together a proposal for a prospective client, a mid-size commercial property insurance broker with about 40 offices across the US Midwest. She has a good sense of their business from the intro call but no current read on the industry pressures they're facing right now.

She opens Gemini, starts a new Deep Research session, and enters the industry-research prompt: INDUSTRY is "commercial property insurance brokerage," GEOGRAPHY/MARKET is "US Midwest," COMPANY SIZE/TYPE is "regional brokers with 20-60 offices," and SPECIFIC ANGLE is "rising reinsurance costs and their effect on client retention."

Before running, Gemini shows Priya its proposed research plan — a short list of the sub-questions and source types it intends to check. She edits one step that was drifting toward national data instead of Midwest-specific data, then lets it run.

A few minutes later, Deep Research returns three cited trends — reinsurance rate increases passed through to commercial clients, a wave of consolidation among regional brokers, and a shift toward digital-first client onboarding — each with a source and publish date, plus two named regional competitors and a note flagging that one figure about market consolidation came from a national dataset rather than a Midwest-specific one.

Priya opens two of the cited sources herself to confirm they're accurate and recent. One, from eight months ago, checks out; the other, on the consolidation trend, turns out to cover the Southeast, not the Midwest, so she drops that point rather than using it. She asks a follow-up inside the same research thread to narrow the consolidation trend specifically to Midwest data, and gets a clearer, smaller but genuinely regional answer back.

She compiles the two solid trends into a three-sentence "why now" section for the proposal. Total time: about twenty minutes, including reviewing the research plan and opening source links.

placeholders.name: PASTE OUTLINE
placeholders.what: Paste your already-locked storyline outline here — the section order you decided on earlier (for example, from the storyline-structuring step), not a new structure. This tells the AI what order the slides need to build toward, so the action titles connect logically rather than reading as disconnected headlines.
examples:
1. Situation: retention has declined steadily for 3 quarters
2. Complication: the drop is concentrated in one segment and one channel
3. Resolution: a targeted retention program for that segment, with a rollout plan

1. Problem: fulfillment costs from Warehouse A are rising
2. Cause: capacity imbalance and an unfavorable new carrier contract
3. Solution: partial consolidation into Warehouse B with a phased timeline

placeholders.name: SLIDE 1 – LABEL
placeholders.what: A short internal label for the first slide so you and the AI both know which slide you're referring to — this isn't the final slide title, just a working name like "Retention trend" or "Cost comparison."
examples: Retention trend by segment
Warehouse capacity comparison
Onboarding completion rates

placeholders.name: CONTENT
placeholders.what: The actual data point, chart description, or finding that slide is built around — specific numbers and facts, not a vague topic description. This is what the AI checks the action title against, so vague content here produces an action title that can't be trusted.
examples: Chart shows monthly churn rate by segment over 6 quarters. Churn in the under-$10K ARR segment rose from 9% to 22%; churn in the $50K+ segment stayed flat at 5-6% throughout.
Table comparing Warehouse A and B: A is at 94% capacity with an 18% shipping cost increase this year; B is at 61% capacity with flat shipping costs.
Bar chart of onboarding completion by week: only 40% of new hires finish onboarding within 30 days; average time to complete is 52 days.

placeholders.name: SLIDE 2 – LABEL
placeholders.what: The working label for your second slide, following the same short naming pattern as the first. Continue adding a [SLIDE N – LABEL]: [CONTENT] pair for every additional slide in your deck beyond the two shown in the template.
examples: Root cause: support response time
Carrier contract cost breakdown
Manager time spent on manual onboarding

variations.label: Executive summary only, no slide titles
variations.whenToUse: You already have solid slide titles you're happy with and just need the one-page executive summary written from the locked content — a common case when the deck was mostly finished before you thought to write the cover summary.
variations.prompt:
I have a finished set of consulting slides with locked titles and content. Write only a one-page executive summary — no slide titles needed.

Storyline / section order: [PASTE OUTLINE]

Slide titles and content:
[SLIDE 1 TITLE]: [CONTENT]
[SLIDE 2 TITLE]: [CONTENT]
...(continue for all slides)

Write a one-page executive summary: situation, 2-3 key findings, recommendation, next steps — using ONLY the content provided, no new claims. Keep it under 300 words and written for someone who will only read this page, not the full deck.

variations.label: Confidence-rated version
variations.whenToUse: You want to know, before the deck goes to review, which action titles rest on strong evidence versus which ones are the shakiest, so you know exactly where to spend your limited review time.
variations.prompt:
I have a set of consulting slides with locked content. Write action titles and rate each one's evidence strength.

Storyline / section order: [PASTE OUTLINE]

For each slide, here is the content:
[SLIDE 1 – LABEL]: [CONTENT]
[SLIDE 2 – LABEL]: [CONTENT]
...(continue for all slides)

For each slide: write an action title under 15 words stating the conclusion, then rate the evidence behind it as Strong / Moderate / Weak based only on the content given, with one sentence explaining the rating. List the Weak-rated titles separately at the end as "revisit before sending."

variations.label: One-liner version for a status update, not a full deck
variations.whenToUse: You're writing a short recurring update (a weekly readout, a steering committee one-pager) rather than a full slide deck, and just need the same conclusion-first discipline applied to a shorter format.
variations.prompt:
I have findings for a short status update, not a full slide deck. Help me write it with the same discipline as good slide titles: lead with the conclusion, not the topic.

Findings: [PASTE FINDINGS]

Write 4-5 bullet points, each leading with the conclusion in the first few words (not "Update on X" but the actual finding), followed by one supporting detail. Flag any bullet where the conclusion is stronger than what the finding actually supports.

followUps.label: Check for causation vs. correlation
followUps.prompt: Go through each action title again and specifically check: does any of them imply that one thing caused another, when the underlying content only shows they happened at the same time or moved together? Flag those and suggest a more accurate, still punchy alternative title.

followUps.label: Read the titles as a standalone story
followUps.prompt: List just the action titles, in order, with no other text. Read them as if they were the only thing a rushed executive saw. Does the sequence tell a coherent, complete story from problem to recommendation? If there's a logical gap between any two titles, point out exactly where.

followUps.label: Tighten the executive summary further
followUps.prompt: Cut the executive summary to under 120 words without losing the recommendation or the strongest supporting finding. If something has to go, drop supporting detail before dropping the recommendation or next steps.

followUps.label: Make the titles punchier without overstating them
followUps.prompt: Rewrite the action titles to be more direct and specific — cut hedge words like 'may' or 'could indicate' only where the underlying content genuinely supports a firmer claim. Where the content is genuinely uncertain, keep the hedge rather than remove it just for punchiness.

con-i2-slide-narratives-executive-summar.walkthrough:
Rosa has finished the analysis for a customer-retention engagement and has seven slides of finished charts and data, but every slide currently has a placeholder title like "Retention Analysis" and "Segment Breakdown" — accurate about the topic, useless as a headline.

She opens Claude and pastes her locked storyline outline (situation, complication, resolution) followed by all seven slides, each as a [SLIDE N – LABEL]: [CONTENT] pair, with the actual chart data and numbers typed out under each one — not just "chart showing churn," but the real figures: churn by segment, response-time data, the proposed program's projected cost.

Claude returns seven action titles. One reads "Churn among small accounts nearly tripled in three quarters, from 9% to 22%." Another gets flagged: the drafted title implied that slow support response time caused the churn increase, but the underlying content only shows the two trends moved together in the same period — a real distinction Rosa hadn't caught while deep in the analysis. It also produces a one-page executive summary and lists all seven titles alone at the end.

Rosa reads the standalone title list out loud, and it holds together as a story. She sends the causation/correlation follow-up as a final check, and Claude confirms the one flagged title was the only issue — the rest are supported. She rewrites that one title to say the two trends "moved together," not that one caused the other, before the deck goes to her partner for review.

The whole pass, from pasting the seven slides to a corrected title list, took about eighteen minutes — considerably faster than the usual half-day spent staring at a blank title bar per slide.

placeholders.name: 1:1 interview / group workshop
placeholders.what: State which format this is — a one-on-one conversation with a single stakeholder, or a group session with multiple people at once. This changes the whole shape of the guide: a 1:1 can go deeper on one person's perspective, while a workshop needs facilitation structure to manage the room.
examples: 1:1 interview
group workshop

placeholders.name: STATE IT
placeholders.what: Name the specific hypothesis or open question this conversation needs to help answer — not the general topic of the engagement, but the actual thing you're trying to find out or confirm. A sharp hypothesis produces sharp, non-generic questions.
examples: Operations leadership believes the new ERP rollout caused fulfillment delays, but frontline staff may see a different root cause
Sales leadership suspects the new pricing tier is confusing prospects during the sales cycle, but the sales team hasn't confirmed this directly
We think onboarding delays are driven by a bottleneck in manager approvals, not a lack of training materials

placeholders.name: ROLE, WHAT THEY LIKELY KNOW OR ARE SENSITIVE ABOUT
placeholders.what: Describe who you're talking to and be honest about what they're likely to be defensive or guarded about — this is what lets the AI predict realistic deflective answers and prepare you a genuinely useful follow-up probe instead of a generic one.
examples: Warehouse shift supervisor, likely defensive about their team's performance and unlikely to volunteer staffing problems unprompted
VP of Sales, protective of the current pricing strategy since they championed it, may downplay early confusion signals
Frontline customer support rep, candid about workload but nervous about criticizing their manager directly

placeholders.name: MINUTES
placeholders.what: State how much time you actually have for this conversation, in minutes — this determines how many questions the guide should realistically include and which ones get marked for cutting first if time runs short.

placeholders.name: 1:1 interview / group workshop, and group size if applicable
placeholders.what: Restate the format, and if it's a workshop, add roughly how many people will be in the room — group size changes the facilitation approach significantly (5 people versus 20 need very different structures).
examples: 1:1 interview
group workshop, approximately 8 participants
group workshop, approximately 20 participants across 3 breakout tables

placeholders.name: X minutes
placeholders.what: This is a threshold you set for the AI to use when deciding what to cut if the conversation runs short — for example, telling it "if time is under 20 minutes" so it knows which questions are safe to drop first without you having to decide live, under pressure, mid-conversation.

variations.label: Follow-up debrief after the interview
variations.whenToUse: You've already run the interview and have raw notes, and want to turn those notes into a structured read on what was confirmed, contradicted, or still unclear relative to your original hypothesis.
variations.prompt:
I just finished a stakeholder interview. Here's the original hypothesis it was meant to test: [STATE THE HYPOTHESIS]

Here are my raw notes from the conversation:
[PASTE YOUR RAW NOTES]

Go through the notes and tell me: 1) what confirms the hypothesis, 2) what contradicts it, 3) what's still genuinely unclear and needs another source to resolve. Use only what's in my notes — do not infer beyond what was actually said.

variations.label: Sensitive-topic version with extra care on framing
variations.whenToUse: The interview touches something the stakeholder may be personally sensitive about (a mistake their team made, a decision they championed that isn't working) and you need extra care in how questions are framed to get an honest answer without putting them on the defensive.
variations.prompt:
I'm preparing for a [1:1 interview / group workshop] on a sensitive topic as part of a consulting engagement.

Open hypothesis / question this needs to help answer: [STATE IT]
Interviewee role and context: [ROLE, WHAT THEY LIKELY KNOW OR ARE SENSITIVE ABOUT]
Why this is sensitive: [E.G. "THEY CHAMPIONED THE DECISION WE'RE NOW QUESTIONING"]
Time available: [MINUTES]

Give me a sequenced guide where every core question is framed to invite an honest answer without sounding like an accusation — for example, asking about the conditions and constraints they were working under rather than asking directly why something didn't work. For each question, include the deflective answer most likely given the sensitivity, and a specific, non-confrontational follow-up probe.

variations.label: Quick pre-call refresher, five minutes before you walk in
variations.whenToUse: You already prepared a full guide earlier, but you're walking into the room in five minutes and want a condensed, glanceable version, not the full document.
variations.prompt:
Condense this interview guide into a single half-page cheat sheet I can glance at right before I walk in: the hypothesis in one line, the 3 highest-priority questions only, and the single most likely deflection with its probe for each. Cut everything else.

[PASTE YOUR FULL GUIDE]

followUps.label: Add a second layer of probes
followUps.prompt: For the two questions most central to the hypothesis, give me a second follow-up probe in case the first one also gets deflected — I want a backup, not just one attempt at getting a concrete answer.

followUps.label: Tighten for a shorter slot
followUps.prompt: My time slot just got cut to [NEW MINUTES] minutes. Rebuild the cut list — tell me exactly which questions to drop first, and confirm the remaining ones still let me test the core hypothesis.

followUps.label: Make the opening warm-up less generic
followUps.prompt: The warm-up questions feel generic. Rewrite them to reference something specific about this person's actual role or the current situation, so the conversation doesn't open on autopilot small talk.

followUps.label: Turn my notes into a hypothesis update after the interview
followUps.prompt: Here are my raw notes from the interview: [PASTE NOTES]. Tell me which parts of the original hypothesis were confirmed, contradicted, or still unclear, using only what's actually in these notes.

con-i3-workshop-interview-preparation.walkthrough:
Kevin is a consultant investigating why a client's new ERP rollout coincided with a spike in fulfillment delays. Operations leadership is convinced the ERP is the cause. Kevin isn't sure, and he has a 30-minute 1:1 scheduled with a warehouse shift supervisor who, from what he's heard, tends to get defensive when performance comes up.

He opens Claude and fills in the prompt: format is 1:1 interview, the hypothesis is that leadership believes the ERP rollout caused the delays but frontline staff may see it differently, the interviewee is a warehouse shift supervisor likely defensive about their team's numbers, and time available is 30 minutes.

The guide comes back with two warm-up questions, five core questions probing the transition period without directly blaming the team, and one closing open question. For a question about whether the new system slowed down daily workflows, it predicts the supervisor might deflect with something like "we've just been short-staffed lately" and supplies a specific probe: ask for the exact week staffing levels changed, to separate a staffing issue from a system issue. It also marks which two questions to cut first if the conversation runs past 20 minutes.

Kevin walks in with the guide open on his laptop. Sure enough, the supervisor's first answer is close to the predicted deflection about staffing. Kevin uses the rehearsed probe, asking for the specific week, and gets a concrete answer: staffing had actually been stable, but two of the four warehouse terminals stopped supporting the new ERP's barcode scanner, forcing manual entry.

After the call, Kevin pastes his raw notes back into Claude asking what was confirmed versus contradicted relative to the original hypothesis — the ERP theory holds, but the specific mechanism turns out to be a hardware compatibility gap, not a training or workflow problem. Preparation and debrief together took about twenty-five minutes.

placeholders.name:
PASTE ROUGH NOTES, e.g.:
- Kickoff/document review: synthesize client documents into a briefing using [TOOL]
- Research: industry/competitor research using [TOOL]
- Storyline: structure findings into a narrative using [TOOL]
- Deliverable drafting: slide action titles and executive summary using [TOOL]
- Interview/workshop prep: question guides using [TOOL]
- Client review: (describe if AI is used here)
- Close-out: (describe if AI is used here)
placeholders.what: List your engagement's actual stages in order, and for each one, note in plain language whether and how AI currently helps — the example format shows one line per stage. Keep the stages honest to how your team actually works today, not an idealized version; leave a stage's description blank or write "no AI used here" if that's the truth.
examples:
- Kickoff/document review: synthesize client documents into a briefing using Claude
- Research: industry/competitor research using Gemini Deep Research
- Storyline: structure findings into a narrative using Claude
- Deliverable drafting: slide action titles and executive summary using Claude
- Interview/workshop prep: question guides using ChatGPT
- Client review: no AI used, all manual partner review
- Close-out: no AI used currently

- Kickoff/document review: not yet using AI for this, done manually by the engagement lead
- Research: competitor and market research using Gemini Deep Research
- Storyline: no AI used, whiteboarded by the team
- Deliverable drafting: slide titles and exec summary drafted with Claude, then heavily edited
- Interview/workshop prep: question guides drafted with ChatGPT
- Client review: no AI
- Close-out: lessons-learned memo drafted with Claude from raw notes

placeholders.name: PASTE OR STATE POLICY, e.g. "no real client-identifying data in any consumer AI account; de-identified excerpts only"
placeholders.what: State your firm's actual data-handling rule for AI tools — what's allowed in a consumer AI account versus what requires de-identifying first or isn't allowed at all. If your firm doesn't have a written policy yet, state the rule you're personally applying until one exists, and flag internally that a real policy is needed.
examples: No real client-identifying data in any consumer AI account; only de-identified excerpts or publicly available material may be pasted in
Client-approved enterprise AI accounts (with a signed data processing agreement) may use real client data; personal/free-tier accounts may only use de-identified or public data
No client financial data or personal employee information in any AI tool under any circumstances; general findings and structure only

placeholders.name: TOOL
placeholders.what: Name the specific AI tool your team uses at that stage — this doesn't need to be the same tool for every stage, and it's fine to leave a stage's tool blank if no AI is used there yet.
examples: Claude
Gemini Deep Research
ChatGPT

variations.label: Single-stage deep dive
variations.whenToUse: You don't want to formalize the whole engagement yet — you just want one specific stage (say, research) written up properly with verification and confidentiality rules before rolling it out team-wide.
variations.prompt:
Turn my notes on one engagement stage into a formal row I can add to our workflow document.

Stage: [NAME THE STAGE, e.g. "Research"]
How AI currently helps: [DESCRIBE]
Tool used: [TOOL]

Produce: Stage | AI-Assisted Task | Tool Used | Required Human Verification | Confidentiality Rule.
The verification column must be a specific, checkable action, not a vague instruction like "review carefully." The confidentiality column should state, based on this policy — [PASTE OR STATE POLICY] — exactly what data is safe to use in this tool at this stage.

variations.label: Gap-analysis version
variations.whenToUse: You want to specifically identify which stages of the engagement have NO defined AI workflow or verification step yet, rather than formalize what's already working — useful before a team meeting about where to invest next.
variations.prompt:
Here are my rough notes on our engagement stages and how AI currently helps (or doesn't) at each:
[PASTE ROUGH NOTES]

Our data-handling policy: [PASTE OR STATE POLICY]

Instead of building the full table, first tell me: which stages have no AI-assisted workflow at all, which stages use AI but have no defined verification step, and which stages have both a workflow and clear verification. Rank the gaps by how much time or risk you'd guess is at stake, based only on what I've described — flag clearly that this ranking is your estimate, not a confirmed fact.

variations.label: New-hire training version
variations.whenToUse: The workflow document already exists and you want it rewritten as an onboarding walkthrough for a new team member, rather than a reference table for people who already know the context.
variations.prompt:
Here is our finished engagement workflow table:
[PASTE YOUR WORKFLOW TABLE]

Rewrite this as a short onboarding walkthrough for a new team member who has never used any of these tools professionally — explain, in plain language, what to do at each stage, why the verification step matters (not just what it is), and what happens if the confidentiality rule is skipped. Keep it under 500 words.

followUps.label: Check verification steps aren't vague
followUps.prompt: Go back through every row's "Required Human Verification" column and flag any that isn't a specific, checkable action a new team member could actually perform without guessing what "review carefully" means in practice.

followUps.label: Stress-test against a real recent engagement
followUps.prompt: Here's a summary of a real engagement we just ran: [DESCRIBE ENGAGEMENT]. Walk through the workflow table stage by stage and tell me anywhere this real engagement didn't actually match the documented workflow — either a stage we skipped, a tool we didn't use, or a verification step we didn't actually do.

followUps.label: Add a stage we missed
followUps.prompt: We also have a [STAGE NAME] stage that I didn't originally describe. Here's how it works: [DESCRIBE]. Add it to the table in the right position, following the same format and level of specificity as the other rows.

followUps.label: Simplify for a one-page poster version
followUps.prompt: Condense this into a one-page version simple enough to post near a shared desk — just stage name, tool, and the single most important verification action per stage, dropping the confidentiality column into a separate short list below the table.

con-a1-repeatable-engagement-workflow.walkthrough:
Elena leads a five-person consulting team where everyone has picked up their own AI habits — she uses Claude for briefings, one analyst swears by Gemini Deep Research, another still writes storylines by hand. Nothing is written down, and a new analyst joining next month will have to learn all of it by osmosis.

Elena blocks 30 minutes and writes rough notes on six stages: kickoff/document review (Claude, for briefings), research (Gemini Deep Research), storyline (Claude, sometimes skipped in favor of whiteboarding), deliverable drafting (Claude, for slide titles and exec summaries), interview prep (ChatGPT), and client review and close-out, both currently done with no AI at all. She also writes down the firm's actual, if informal, data rule: no real client-identifying data in anyone's personal AI account, de-identified excerpts only.

She pastes both into the prompt. The output comes back as a six-row table (client review and close-out both correctly marked "no AI-assisted task currently" instead of inventing one), each row with a genuinely specific verification action — for research, "open and confirm the top 3 cited sources before use in a client-facing document"; for storyline, "confirm no finding was reframed as stronger evidence than the raw data supports." Every row's confidentiality column consistently applies the de-identified-only rule.

Elena runs the stress-test follow-up against last month's actual engagement and catches one gap: the team used Claude for interview prep on that project, not ChatGPT as she'd assumed, so she corrects the table. She circulates the finished one-pager to the team and pins it above the storyline-structuring lesson as the team's new shared reference. Total time: about 35 minutes.

placeholders.name: MEETING NAME/TOPIC
placeholders.what: A short name identifying which meeting this is — useful mainly so the summary is easy to find and reference later, especially if you run this same process weekly.
examples: Weekly Sprint Planning
Vendor Integration Kickoff
Q1 Budget Review with Finance

placeholders.name: DATE
placeholders.what: The date the meeting happened, so the record is unambiguous later when someone asks "which meeting was that decision made in."
examples: March 3, 2026
Jan 14

placeholders.name: LIST
placeholders.what: The names of everyone who attended the meeting, so the AI can correctly attribute actions to actual people mentioned in your notes rather than guessing who was in the room.
examples: Sarah Chen, Tom Reyes, Priya Nair, you
Full engineering team + Product (6 people)
Client: Mark Douglas (CFO); Internal: you, Lena

placeholders.name: PASTE RAW NOTES
placeholders.what: Your actual raw notes from the meeting, in whatever shorthand you naturally use — messy is fine, and even preferred, since a cleaned-up summary loses the specific details (who said what) that the AI needs to correctly assign owners and dates.
examples: agreed to push launch to March 15, Sarah will update the timeline doc by Friday, still need to decide on vendor for the integration - Tom to get 2 more quotes, discussed budget overrun but no resolution

reviewed Q1 numbers, revenue on target but marketing spend over by 8%. Priya to send breakdown by EOD Thurs. Decided to pause the paid ads test. Open question: do we reallocate budget to email or hold it.

client wants 2 extra dashboard views added, we said yes but flagged it needs a separate change order - Mark to send updated SOW, no date given. Also agreed current sprint stays as-is, no scope change mid-sprint.

variations.label: Quick voice-memo version
variations.whenToUse: You didn't take structured notes and instead have a rough voice memo transcript or a stream-of-consciousness recap you typed right after the meeting ended.
variations.prompt:
I recorded a quick voice memo recap right after a meeting instead of taking notes during it. Turn this into a structured record. Use ONLY what's stated below — do not invent a decision, owner, or deadline that isn't mentioned. If an action item has no clear owner or date, write "TBD."

Meeting: [MEETING NAME/TOPIC], [DATE]

My recap (rough, spoken style):
[PASTE YOUR ROUGH RECAP OR TRANSCRIPT]

Structure the output as: 1) Decisions made, 2) Action items (Action | Owner | Due date), 3) Open issues, 4) One-sentence summary at the top.

variations.label: Recurring meeting with a previous action-item check-in
variations.whenToUse: This is a recurring meeting (weekly standup, biweekly steering committee) and you want the new summary to also flag whether previous action items were closed out, not just capture new ones.
variations.prompt:
Turn my raw meeting notes into a structured record, and also check the status of last meeting's open action items.

Meeting: [MEETING NAME/TOPIC], [DATE]
Attendees: [LIST]

Last meeting's open action items:
[PASTE PREVIOUS ACTION ITEMS: ACTION | OWNER | DUE DATE]

This meeting's raw notes:
[PASTE RAW NOTES]

Structure the output as:
1. Status of previous action items (Done / Still open / No update given — based only on what's in this meeting's notes, don't assume completion without evidence)
2. New decisions made
3. New action items (Action | Owner | Due date, use "TBD" where not stated)
4. Open issues / parking lot
5. One-sentence summary at the top

variations.label: Owner-specific extract
variations.whenToUse: You need to quickly pull out just one person's action items to paste into a direct message to them, rather than sending the whole meeting summary to everyone.
variations.prompt:
From these raw meeting notes, pull out only the action items belonging to [PERSON'S NAME] — nothing else. Use ONLY what's stated; if no clear due date was given, write "TBD" rather than guessing one.

Raw notes:
[PASTE RAW NOTES]

Format as a short numbered list I can paste directly into a Slack or email message to this person, with a one-sentence friendly opener.

followUps.label: Check nothing was misattributed
followUps.prompt: Go back through my raw notes line by line and confirm every action item's owner is actually the person named in the notes, not inferred from who seems most relevant to the task. List any action item where you had to guess.

followUps.label: Separate settled decisions from ones that still need sign-off
followUps.prompt: Look again at the 'Decisions made' section — are any of these actually still pending a final sign-off or approval rather than fully settled? If so, move them to open issues instead, since listing something as decided when it isn't creates false certainty.

followUps.label: Draft the send-out message
followUps.prompt: Write a short email or Slack message to send this summary to the attendees — 2-3 sentences introducing it, then paste the structured summary below. Keep the tone brief and neutral, not overly formal.

followUps.label: Flag anything ambiguous I should double check
followUps.prompt: Reread my raw notes and flag anything that was genuinely ambiguous — where you weren't fully sure if something was a firm decision, a suggestion, or just a comment in passing — so I can clarify it with the room before sending this out.

pm-b1-meeting-notes-to-decisions-actions.walkthrough:
James runs a weekly cross-functional sync for a product launch and, like most PMs, is bad about writing up notes afterward — they usually sit in a notebook until someone asks "wait, who owns that?"

Right after this week's meeting, while it's still fresh, he opens ChatGPT and pastes the prompt. Meeting name is "Launch Readiness Sync," date is today, attendees are Sarah, Tom, and Priya. His raw notes, typed exactly as scrawled during the call: "agreed to push launch to March 15, Sarah will update the timeline doc by Friday, still need to decide on vendor for the integration - Tom to get 2 more quotes, discussed budget overrun but no resolution."

The output comes back in under ten seconds: a one-sentence summary at the top noting the launch date moved and vendor selection is still open; a decisions section with one bullet, "Launch date moved to March 15"; an action items table with two rows — "Update timeline doc — Sarah — Friday" and "Get 2 more vendor quotes — Tom — TBD," correctly leaving the date blank since James never gave one; and an open issues section listing the vendor decision and the unresolved budget overrun.

James reads it against his raw notes in about thirty seconds — everything matches. He sends a quick follow-up asking ChatGPT to draft the Slack message to send it out, and gets a short two-sentence opener plus the summary formatted for Slack, ready to paste. He posts it in the team channel four minutes after the meeting ended, while everyone else is still at their desks — instead of the usual next-day (or never) writeup that made people ask what they were supposed to be doing.

placeholders.name: NAME
placeholders.what: The name of the project this status report is about — use whatever name your stakeholders already recognize, so there's no confusion about which initiative this covers.
examples: Customer Portal Redesign
Q2 Vendor Migration
Regional Expansion – Phase 1

placeholders.name: DATES
placeholders.what: The specific date range this report covers, so stakeholders know exactly what period the update reflects and can tell if a report is late or current.
examples: Feb 3 - Feb 9, 2026
January 2026
Sprint 14 (Jan 26 - Feb 8)

placeholders.name: ON TRACK / AT RISK / OFF TRACK
placeholders.what: Your own honest judgment of the project's status — not something to let the AI infer from your notes. Decide this first, based on your actual assessment, since this single word sets the tone stakeholders will read the rest of the report through.
examples: ON TRACK
AT RISK
OFF TRACK

placeholders.name: ROUGH NOTES
placeholders.what: Your own quick, unpolished notes on what actually happened or what's actually planned — bullet fragments are fine, full sentences aren't required. This appears twice in the prompt: once for what happened this period, once for what's planned next period.
examples: finished 2 of 3 integration milestones, vendor testing started late, held the design review Tuesday, got sign-off on the new nav
start UAT with 5 pilot users, finalize the rollout comms plan, vendor delivers remaining API by Friday (their commitment, not confirmed yet)

placeholders.name: ROUGH NOTES, or "none"
placeholders.what: Your rough notes on any current blockers or risks — or literally the word "none" if there genuinely aren't any this period. Don't invent a risk just to fill the section; an honest "none this period" is a valid and useful answer.
examples: vendor is 2 weeks behind with no committed recovery date, this threatens the March 15 launch
none
one pilot user reported a login bug, engineering is investigating, not yet clear if it's isolated

placeholders.name: DECISION NEEDED / APPROVAL NEEDED / FYI ONLY, be specific
placeholders.what: State exactly what you need from the person reading this report — a specific decision, a specific approval, or nothing at all beyond awareness. Vague asks like "let me know your thoughts" get ignored; a specific ask gets a faster response.
examples: Need your approval to escalate the vendor delay to their account manager this week
FYI only — no action needed, just keeping you informed of the milestone completion
Need a decision by Friday on whether to delay launch 1 week or launch with the known bug and patch after

variations.label: Ultra-short version for a busy exec sponsor
variations.whenToUse: Your stakeholder genuinely only wants 3 lines, not even the standard 200-word format — common for a very senior sponsor who gets a dozen of these a week.
variations.prompt:
Write an extremely short project status update — no more than 3 lines total — for a busy executive sponsor.

Project: [NAME]
Overall status: [ON TRACK / AT RISK / OFF TRACK] — use exactly this, do not soften it.
Most important thing that happened: [ONE FACT]
Most important thing needed from the reader, if anything: [STATE IT, OR "nothing"]

Line 1: status + one-sentence reason. Line 2: the most important fact. Line 3: the ask, or "No action needed." Nothing else — no headers, no bullet list.

variations.label: Multi-project rollup version
variations.whenToUse: You manage several projects and need one combined report covering all of them for a stakeholder who oversees the portfolio, not a single-project deep dive.
variations.prompt:
Write a combined status report covering multiple projects for a portfolio-level stakeholder, skimmable in under two minutes.

Reporting period: [DATES]

For each project, I'll give you: name, status, and one line on what matters.
[PROJECT 1 NAME]: [ON TRACK/AT RISK/OFF TRACK] — [ONE-LINE WHY]
[PROJECT 2 NAME]: [ON TRACK/AT RISK/OFF TRACK] — [ONE-LINE WHY]
...(continue for all projects)

Structure: one line per project, status-flagged clearly at the start of each line (use the status I gave you, don't infer or soften it), sorted with AT RISK and OFF TRACK projects at the top. End with a single line noting which projects need something from the reader, if any.

variations.label: Detailed internal version for your own team
variations.whenToUse: You want a more detailed version for internal team visibility (not the external stakeholder-facing report) that includes more granular detail than the 200-word external version allows.
variations.prompt:
Write a more detailed internal status update for the project team (not external stakeholders) — this can be longer and more granular than a stakeholder report.

Project: [NAME]
Reporting period: [DATES]
Overall status: [ON TRACK / AT RISK / OFF TRACK]

What happened this period (detailed): [ROUGH NOTES]
What's planned next period (detailed): [ROUGH NOTES]
Blockers/risks, with who's working on each: [ROUGH NOTES]

Structure: status line, then a fuller "this period" section (up to 8 bullets), a fuller "next period" section, a risks section with an owner noted per risk, and a short "decisions/help needed" section. Do not soften the stated status. This version can run longer than 200 words since it's for the team, not external stakeholders.

followUps.label: Check the status line actually matches the content
followUps.prompt: Reread the risks/blockers section you wrote. Does it genuinely support the status I gave you, or does the content actually read more serious (or less serious) than the status label suggests? Tell me honestly, don't just agree with my stated status.

followUps.label: Cut it down further
followUps.prompt: This is still too long. Cut it to under 120 words total without losing the status line or the specific ask. Cut supporting detail first, not the ask.

followUps.label: Make the ask impossible to miss
followUps.prompt: Move the 'what I need from you' line to the very top of the report, right after the status line, instead of the bottom — for a stakeholder skimming fast, the ask needs to be one of the first things they see.

followUps.label: Write the one-line version for a subject line
followUps.prompt: Give me a single email subject line, under 10 words, that captures this report's status and most important point — something a stakeholder could act on just from their inbox preview without opening the email.

pm-b2-status-reports-stakeholders-read.walkthrough:
Amir manages a customer portal redesign project and it's Friday, report day. The project has genuinely slipped this week — a vendor delivery is two weeks late — and Amir has caught himself in the past writing "on track" out of habit because admitting risk feels like inviting a hard conversation. This week he decides not to do that.

He opens Claude and fills in the prompt honestly: project name is "Customer Portal Redesign," reporting period is this week's dates, and — deliberately, before touching anything else — he types the status as AT RISK. His rough notes: this period covered finishing two of three integration milestones and a design review sign-off; next period covers starting UAT with pilot users, pending the vendor; the blocker is the vendor's remaining API delivery, now two weeks late with no committed recovery date, threatening the March 15 launch date; and what he needs is the executive sponsor's approval to escalate to the vendor's account manager.

Claude returns a report under 200 words: a status line reading "AT RISK — vendor delivery slippage threatens the March 15 launch," three bullets on what happened, three on what's next, a blockers section naming the vendor delay specifically with the two-week figure, and a closing line: "Need: your approval to escalate to the vendor's account manager this week."

Amir sends a follow-up asking Claude to check honestly whether the content matches the AT RISK label — it confirms the content is consistent, maybe even understated. He sends the report as-is. The sponsor replies within the hour approving the escalation — the fastest response he's gotten to a status report in months. Total time: nine minutes.

placeholders.name: ONE-SENTENCE GOAL
placeholders.what: State the project's actual goal in one clear sentence — the outcome, not the process. This is what everything else in the plan gets built around, so a vague goal here produces a vague, unusable plan.
examples: Launch a redesigned customer self-service portal by end of Q3
Migrate all customer data from the legacy CRM to the new platform with zero data loss
Open and staff a second regional warehouse capable of handling 40% of current order volume

placeholders.name: DATE
placeholders.what: The target completion date for the whole project — the deadline you're planning backward from, not a milestone date.
examples: September 30, 2026
End of Q3 2026
March 15, 2026

placeholders.name: BUDGET / TEAM SIZE / FIXED EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES
placeholders.what: Your real, hard constraints — the things that aren't negotiable and will shape what's actually feasible. Naming these upfront keeps the plan grounded in reality instead of an idealized version with unlimited resources.
examples: Team of 6 (2 engineers, 1 designer, 1 PM, 2 support), budget capped at $85K for external vendors, hard dependency on a third-party auth vendor's API which won't be ready until June
No dedicated engineering resource until Q2, must use existing warehouse management software (no new procurement approved), fixed launch date tied to a signed customer contract
Team of 3, no external budget approved yet (pending a separate approval), dependent on Legal's review which typically takes 3-4 weeks

placeholders.name: AFTER I ANSWER:
placeholders.what: This isn't a value you type in — it's a stage marker built into the prompt telling both you and the AI that Step 2 (building the actual breakdown) only happens after you've answered the Step 1 clarifying questions. Think of the prompt as two messages, not one: send everything up through Step 1 first, wait for the questions back, then continue.
examples: Paste the prompt as-is (Step 1 only will run, since you haven't answered anything yet), read the clarifying questions the AI asks, then reply in the same conversation with your answers to trigger Step 2
If the AI tries to jump straight to a full breakdown without asking questions, reply "Please ask your clarifying questions first before building the plan" to force it back to Step 1
Keep this as one continuous conversation rather than two separate chats — Step 2 needs the context of your Step 1 answers to build an accurate breakdown

placeholders.name: from my input
placeholders.what: You don't fill this in either — it's a tag the AI attaches to individual tasks in its output to mark which ones came directly from something you actually told it (your goal, your constraints, or your answers to the clarifying questions), as opposed to a guess. Seeing this tag next to a task means you can trust it without double-checking it against your own knowledge.
examples: Integrate with [Vendor Name]'s auth API — [from my input]
Complete UAT with the 6-person pilot group you named — [from my input]
Launch by September 30 per your target date — [from my input]

placeholders.name: typical pattern — verify
placeholders.what: The paired tag for tasks the AI added on its own, based on what's common for this type of project, rather than something you specifically told it. It's a flag, not a fact — you're expected to confirm each one against your team's real capacity and process, or delete it if it doesn't actually apply.
examples: Two-week UAT period — [typical pattern — verify]
One-week buffer before launch for final QA — [typical pattern — verify]
Stakeholder sign-off checkpoint at end of design phase — [typical pattern — verify]

variations.label: Skip clarifying questions, generate directly
variations.whenToUse: You already know the project type well (you've run something similar before) and don't need the AI to ask clarifying questions first — you just want a fast first-draft breakdown to correct.
variations.prompt:
I need a first-draft work breakdown structure for a project, to correct and refine myself — not a final plan. Skip clarifying questions and generate directly from what I give you.

Goal: [ONE-SENTENCE GOAL]
Target date: [DATE]
Constraints: [BUDGET / TEAM SIZE / FIXED EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES]
Additional context: [ANYTHING ELSE RELEVANT — team composition, existing systems, prior similar projects]

Produce a phased work breakdown structure: phases in logical order, major tasks under each phase, rough sequencing/dependencies. Mark each task "[from my input]" or "[typical pattern — verify]" so I know which parts to double-check against my own experience with this type of project.

variations.label: Comparison against a similar past project
variations.whenToUse: You've run a similar project before and want the new plan built by comparison to that one, flagging what's genuinely different this time rather than starting from a generic template.
variations.prompt:
I need a work breakdown for a new project, and I want it built by comparing it to a similar one we ran before, not from a generic template.

New project goal: [ONE-SENTENCE GOAL]
Target date: [DATE]
Constraints: [BUDGET / TEAM SIZE / FIXED EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES]

Here's how a similar past project actually went, phases and what took longer or shorter than expected:
[DESCRIBE THE PAST PROJECT AND WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED]

Build the new breakdown using the past project's real phases and sequencing as your primary reference point, adjusting only for what's explicitly different about this new project. Flag anywhere you're deviating from the past project's pattern and why.

variations.label: Just the clarifying questions, no plan yet
variations.whenToUse: You're at the very start of scoping and genuinely don't have enough information yet to build even a first draft — you want a sharp list of questions to bring to a scoping conversation with your sponsor or team first.
variations.prompt:
I'm scoping a new project and want a list of clarifying questions to bring into a scoping conversation, before attempting any plan.

Goal (rough, may be incomplete): [ONE-SENTENCE GOAL]

List the specific questions you'd need answered to build a realistic work breakdown for this — covering team composition, existing systems, approval processes, external dependencies, and anything else genuinely load-bearing for planning this type of project. Group them by category so I can bring an organized list into the conversation.

followUps.label: Push back on an unrealistic-sounding task duration
followUps.prompt: The [TASK NAME] task is estimated at [DURATION]. Based only on what I've told you about our team, does that estimate seem realistic, or is it a generic typical-pattern assumption? If it's a generic assumption, say so plainly rather than defending it.

followUps.label: Re-sequence around a hard external dependency
followUps.prompt: The [EXTERNAL DEPENDENCY] can't be resolved until [DATE], which is later than your current sequencing assumes. Rebuild the sequencing so nothing that depends on it is scheduled to start before then, and tell me what that does to the overall timeline.

followUps.label: Convert to my PM tool's format
followUps.prompt: Reformat this breakdown as a flat task list suitable for importing into [YOUR PM TOOL, e.g. Asana/Jira/Monday] — one row per task, with phase as a tag or section, and dependencies noted in a separate column.

followUps.label: Strip out everything not yet verified
followUps.prompt: Give me a version of this plan with every task still marked "[typical pattern — verify]" removed entirely, so I can see exactly what's left from what I actually specified myself, before I decide which of the removed ones to add back in.

pm-i1-project-plans-work-breakdowns-from.walkthrough:
Nadia is a project manager who just got asked to lead a customer portal redesign — a project type she's never personally run before, though her company has done similar web projects.

She opens ChatGPT and starts the two-step prompt. Goal: "launch a redesigned customer self-service portal by end of Q3." Target date: September 30. Constraints: a team of 6 (2 engineers, 1 designer, 1 PM, 2 support), and a fixed dependency on a third-party authentication vendor whose new API won't be ready until June.

Before building anything, the AI asks clarifying questions: is design work already underway, what's the current portal's tech stack, and what are the vendor's actual SLA terms for the June API delivery. Nadia answers each — design hasn't started, the current portal runs on an older framework that will need partial rebuilding, and the vendor's SLA has no penalty clause for delay, which she flags as a real risk.

The resulting breakdown has five phases: discovery, design, build, integration, and launch. Under integration, there's an explicit dependency noting that integration testing can't start until the vendor delivers their sandbox environment in June — which, given the no-penalty SLA, Nadia now recognizes as the plan's biggest single risk. Several tasks are tagged "[typical pattern — verify]," including a two-week UAT period and a one-week buffer before launch, both flagged for her to check against her team's real track record.

She reviews it against her team's actual capacity, cuts the UAT period to one week based on past projects, and pastes the corrected structure into Jira. Total time from blank page to an importable plan: about 30 minutes, versus a full afternoon she'd normally spend structuring this from scratch.

placeholders.name: SCOPE, TIMELINE, TEAM SIZE, KEY SENSITIVE AREAS
placeholders.what: A brief project summary covering what it involves, how long it runs, how many people are on it, and anything unusually sensitive about it (a new vendor, a tight deadline, a dependency on another team) — this grounds the AI's ratings in your actual project instead of generic assumptions about projects like it.
examples: Six-month system migration to a new ERP, involving a new external vendor we haven't worked with before, team of 8, hard regulatory deadline tied to a compliance filing
Three-month website relaunch, internal team of 4, no new vendors, but tight timeline overlapping with the busiest sales season
Twelve-month facility expansion, cross-functional team of 15 across construction, ops, and IT, dependent on permitting from the local municipality

placeholders.name: LIST YOUR KNOWN RISKS
placeholders.what: The specific risks you already know about for this project, in your own words — real, specific concerns you've actually thought about, not a generic risk checklist. These become the core of the register; the AI only adds to this list in a clearly separate section.
examples: Vendor may not deliver the integration API on time based on their track record with another client; our internal SME on the legacy system is planning to leave the company mid-project; the regulatory filing deadline is fixed and cannot move

Construction permitting could be delayed by the municipality (their average review time has been running long lately); a key contractor is also working another large job that could pull their crew away

Our email migration vendor has had two prior data-loss incidents reported by other customers; the project timeline overlaps with our fiscal year-end close, which usually pulls finance team attention away

variations.label: Post-mortem to living register
variations.whenToUse: A risk you didn't have registered actually happened, and you want to add it (plus similar risks it suggests) to the register going forward, learning from the miss.
variations.prompt:
A risk that wasn't in our register actually happened on this project. I want to add it and think about what else it suggests we might be missing.

What happened: [DESCRIBE THE RISK THAT MATERIALIZED]
Our current register:
[PASTE YOUR EXISTING REGISTER]

Tasks:
1. Add this risk to the register with a Likelihood/Impact rating (Low/Medium/High) and a specific, trigger-based mitigation, marked as "added retroactively."
2. Based only on what actually happened (not generic speculation), suggest 1-2 related risks in the same category that we should consider adding, clearly separated as suggestions to evaluate, not automatically included.

variations.label: Milestone review and close-out pass
variations.whenToUse: You're at a major milestone and want to review the existing register to close out risks that no longer apply, rather than build a new one from scratch.
variations.prompt:
Review our existing risk register at this project milestone and help me close out what no longer applies.

Current register:
[PASTE YOUR EXISTING REGISTER]
What's changed since it was built: [DESCRIBE — e.g. "vendor contract signed with penalty clause," "key person did not leave after all"]

For each existing risk, tell me whether it should stay open, be closed (with a one-line reason based on what changed), or be re-rated given the new information. Do not close a risk unless the update I gave you genuinely resolves it — flag anything ambiguous instead of guessing.

variations.label: Executive-level risk summary
variations.whenToUse: You need a short, non-technical version of the top risks to include in a steering committee deck, not the full working register with every row.
variations.prompt:
From this full risk register, create a short executive summary version for a steering committee deck — just the top 3 risks by combined likelihood and impact.

Full register:
[PASTE YOUR REGISTER]

For each of the top 3: one plain-language sentence describing the risk (no jargon), the mitigation in one sentence, and whether it needs any decision or resource from the steering committee right now. Skip anything Low/Low — this is for people with five minutes, not the full team.

followUps.label: Push back on a vague mitigation
followUps.prompt: The mitigation for [RISK NAME] just says to monitor it. Give me a specific action and a concrete trigger — what exactly should happen, and at what point (a date, a missed milestone, a specific signal) should it kick in?

followUps.label: Verify a risk-suggestion actually applies
followUps.prompt: You suggested [SUGGESTED RISK] as a risk to consider adding. Based only on the project details I gave you, does this genuinely apply to my project, or is it a generic risk for this project type that may not actually fit my situation? Be honest, don't just defend your own suggestion.

followUps.label: Rank by what needs attention first
followUps.prompt: Rank the risks in this register by which ones need action this week versus which can wait for the next milestone review, based on the likelihood, impact, and mitigation triggers already defined.

followUps.label: Assign draft owners based on role
followUps.prompt: For each risk, suggest which role (not a specific person, since I'll assign that myself) would logically own monitoring and acting on it — e.g. the vendor manager, the tech lead, the PM — based on what the risk and mitigation actually involve.

pm-i2-risk-registers-mitigation-drafts.walkthrough:
Deshawn is kicking off a six-month ERP migration with a new vendor the company hasn't worked with before, a team of eight, and a regulatory filing deadline that genuinely cannot move. He knows he should build a risk register but has always found the exercise turns into either a checklist nobody reads or a blank document he never finishes.
