He opens Claude and gives it the project summary — six-month ERP migration, new external vendor, team of 8, hard regulatory deadline — plus three risks he already knows about: the vendor's API delivery might slip based on their track record with another client, his internal subject-matter expert on the legacy system is planning to leave mid-project, and the filing deadline itself is fixed.

The register comes back with all three risks rated using Low/Medium/High: the vendor delay as Medium likelihood/High impact, with a mitigation specifying a biweekly vendor checkpoint call and a trigger to escalate formally if two consecutive milestones slip; the SME departure as High likelihood/High impact, with a mitigation to start documenting their institutional knowledge immediately rather than waiting for a resignation date. Separately, under a clearly marked "risks to consider adding" section, it suggests two categories he hadn't listed: regulatory approval delay and data-migration rollback capability.

Deshawn reviews the two suggestions — the regulatory one genuinely applies, given the fixed deadline, so he adds it to the real register with his own rating. The rollback-capability suggestion doesn't really fit his specific migration approach, so he leaves it out rather than including it just because it was offered.

He assigns real owners to all four risks and adds the register to his biweekly project review. Total time: about fifteen minutes, versus the half-finished document he'd normally have.

placeholders.name: STATE THE FACTS PLAINLY, e.g. "the vendor's delivery slipped 3 weeks, pushing our integration testing start"
placeholders.what: State exactly what happened, in plain factual language — no softening, no over-explaining. This is the core fact the whole message is built around, so get it right and specific before anything else.
examples: the vendor's delivery slipped 3 weeks, pushing our integration testing start
we discovered a scope gap during build: the reporting module wasn't included in the original estimate, adding roughly 3 weeks of work
the current sprint's budget burn is 18% over plan due to unplanned overtime approved to hit last month's deadline

placeholders.name: REASON, without excessive justification
placeholders.what: The factual reason behind what happened, stated briefly — one sentence, not a defense of the decision or a long justification. Over-explaining here tends to read as making excuses rather than informing.
examples: a component shortage on the vendor's side
the original scoping session didn't include a stakeholder who later flagged the reporting requirement as mandatory
we approved overtime last month specifically to avoid missing the client demo date

placeholders.name: CONCRETE NEXT STEP OR RECOVERY PLAN
placeholders.what: What you're actually doing about the situation — a real, concrete action, even if it's partial or doesn't fully solve the problem. This is what turns a bad-news message into an update rather than just a complaint.
examples: running two integration phases in parallel to recover roughly 10 of the 21 lost days
re-scoping the reporting module as a fast-follow release 2 weeks after the main launch, rather than delaying the whole launch
capping overtime for the remainder of the project and reforecasting the budget with the finance team this week

placeholders.name: e.g. "awareness only" / "approval to shift the launch date" / "additional budget approval"
placeholders.what: State exactly what you need from the reader, if anything — a specific approval, a specific decision, or genuinely nothing beyond keeping them informed. A vague or missing ask is one of the most common reasons these messages stall instead of getting resolved.
examples: awareness only, no action needed
approval to notify downstream teams of a revised go-live window this week
additional budget approval of $15K to cover the reporting module fast-follow

placeholders.name: e.g. "executive sponsor" / "full stakeholder group"
placeholders.what: Who the message is going to — this affects tone and how much background detail is appropriate (an executive sponsor may need less operational detail than the full stakeholder group).
examples: executive sponsor
full stakeholder group
client's project lead only

variations.label: Verbal talking points instead of a written message
variations.whenToUse: You need to deliver this news live on a call rather than in writing, and want short talking points you can speak from rather than a message you'd send as-is.
variations.prompt:
Help me prepare talking points for delivering difficult project news live on a call, not a written message.

What happened: [STATE THE FACTS PLAINLY]
Why (briefly, factually): [REASON, without excessive justification]
What we're doing about it: [CONCRETE NEXT STEP OR RECOVERY PLAN]
What I'm asking for: [WHAT YOU NEED FROM THE READER]
Audience: [WHO'S ON THE CALL]

Give me 4-5 short spoken talking points, not full sentences to read verbatim — phrases and key facts I can glance at while speaking naturally. Lead with the fact. Include one likely question this audience might ask and a one-line answer for it. No corporate hedging language.

variations.label: Pre-announcement heads-up to one key stakeholder
variations.whenToUse: Before sending the full message to the whole stakeholder group, you want a shorter, more personal heads-up to one key person first so they're not blindsided in front of others.
variations.prompt:
I'm about to send difficult project news to a full stakeholder group, but first I want a short, personal heads-up message to one key stakeholder so they're not surprised in the group message.

What happened: [STATE THE FACTS PLAINLY]
What we're doing about it: [CONCRETE NEXT STEP OR RECOVERY PLAN]
This specific person: [NAME/ROLE, AND WHY THEY NEED ADVANCE NOTICE]

Write a short, direct, personal message (under 80 words) giving them advance notice before the full group message goes out, with a one-line offer to talk it through before it's sent more broadly if they want to.

variations.label: Written follow-up after a difficult live conversation
variations.whenToUse: You already delivered the news verbally (in a call or meeting) and now need a short written follow-up confirming what was said and agreed, for the record.
variations.prompt:
I already delivered this news verbally in a meeting. Write a short written follow-up confirming what was discussed and agreed, for the record — not breaking the news again as if it's new.

What was discussed: [STATE THE FACTS PLAINLY]
What we agreed on the call: [CONCRETE NEXT STEP OR RECOVERY PLAN, PLUS ANY DECISIONS MADE LIVE]
Audience: [WHO WAS ON THE CALL]

Write it as a brief recap, not a fresh announcement — open with something like "Following up on today's call" rather than restating the bad news as if they haven't heard it. Confirm the agreed next steps and any dates discussed, using only what was actually agreed.

followUps.label: Check for an invented commitment
followUps.prompt: Reread this draft carefully and confirm it doesn't state any specific date, number, or outcome beyond what I actually gave you. If it invented or implied a recovery date I didn't confirm, point out exactly which sentence and I'll fix it.

followUps.label: Make it sound less defensive
followUps.prompt: Read this back as the recipient would. Does any part of it sound defensive or like it's over-justifying what happened rather than just stating it? Rewrite anything that reads that way to be more direct and matter-of-fact.

followUps.label: Sharpen the ask
followUps.prompt: The closing ask still feels a bit soft. Rewrite the final line so it's impossible to misread as optional — state exactly what you need and by when, if there's a deadline for the response.

followUps.label: Shorten further
followUps.prompt: Cut this to under 100 words without losing the fact, the recovery plan, or the ask. If something has to go, cut the reason/context line before cutting the ask or the recovery plan.

pm-i3-stakeholder-communications-difficu.walkthrough:
Fatima is managing a system integration project and just learned the vendor's delivery has slipped three weeks due to a component shortage on their end. She needs to tell the executive sponsor before he hears it secondhand, and she's aware her instinct under pressure is to over-explain and apologize, which she knows tends to read as less confident, not more considerate.

She opens Claude and fills in the difficult-message prompt directly: what happened is the vendor slip pushing integration testing back three weeks; the reason is the component shortage, stated in one clause, not a paragraph; what they're doing about it is running two integration phases in parallel to recover roughly ten of the twenty-one lost days; what she's asking for is approval to notify downstream teams of a revised go-live window; and the audience is the executive sponsor.

The draft comes back at about 120 words. It opens with the fact directly: "The vendor's delivery has slipped three weeks due to a component shortage on their side." It states the recovery plan in one clear sentence, doesn't invent a new specific recovery date beyond what she gave it, and closes with: "I need your approval to notify downstream teams of a revised go-live window this week."

Fatima reads it once as the sponsor would and sends a follow-up asking Claude to check specifically that it didn't invent any commitment — it confirms nothing beyond what she supplied. She sends the message as written. The sponsor replies within twenty minutes with approval, and separately thanks her for being direct instead of burying the news. Total time from finding out about the vendor slip to sending: about twelve minutes.

placeholders.what: The specific AI tool and/or saved prompt you personally use for that task — naming it precisely means a teammate reading this later knows exactly what to open, not just that "AI" was involved somehow.
examples: Claude, meeting-notes prompt

variations.label: New-PM starter version
variations.whenToUse: You're a newer PM without years of accumulated prompts and verification habits yet — you want a starter operating system built from best-practice defaults rather than assembling your own existing patterns.
variations.prompt:
I'm a newer PM and don't yet have my own set of AI-assisted PM prompts and verification habits. Help me build a starter operating system covering the standard recurring PM tasks: meeting notes, status reports, work breakdowns, risk registers, and difficult stakeholder messages.

For each task, propose: a recommended cadence, a suggested tool (Claude or ChatGPT), a one-sentence description of the core prompting principle to follow (e.g. "never let AI guess an owner or date"), and a specific, checkable verification step. Clearly note that this is a starting template I should adjust once I have real experience with what actually needs checking on my own projects — not a finished system.

variations.label: Team rollout version with adoption plan
variations.whenToUse: You've already built your personal operating system and now want to roll it out to a whole PM team, which needs an adoption plan, not just the reference table itself.
variations.prompt:
I have a working PM operating system I use personally, and want to roll it out to my whole team, not just document it for myself.

My operating system:
[PASTE YOUR ASSEMBLED TABLE]

Help me build a short rollout plan: how to introduce this to the team (a working session vs. just sharing the doc), which task to have people adopt first (pick the lowest-risk, highest-frequency one), how to collect feedback on where the templates don't fit someone's specific project type, and a suggested review cadence for updating the document as a team, not just as an individual.

variations.label: Gap-audit version
variations.whenToUse: Before assembling the full system, you want to specifically identify which of your recurring tasks have no consistent AI-assisted approach at all yet, to prioritize which to build first.
variations.prompt:
Before I build a full operating system document, help me audit where I'm inconsistent. Here are my recurring PM tasks and how I currently handle each, in rough terms:
[PASTE YOUR NOTES]

For each task, tell me: do I have a consistent tool/prompt I use every time, or does it vary? Do I have any defined verification step, or am I relying on gut-check review? Rank the tasks by how much a documented, consistent approach would likely help, based only on what I've described — and flag this ranking clearly as your estimate, not a measured fact.

followUps.label: Fill in a missing verification step honestly
followUps.prompt: You flagged that my [TASK NAME] row has no defined verification step. Here's what I actually do, even if it's informal: [DESCRIBE YOUR REAL HABIT]. Turn that into a specific, checkable verification action rather than leaving it as a vague gap or inventing something I don't actually do.

followUps.label: Test it against a real project cycle
followUps.prompt: I just ran this system for one full sprint/reporting period. Here's what actually happened: [DESCRIBE WHAT WORKED, WHAT YOU SKIPPED, WHAT TOOK LONGER THAN EXPECTED]. Update the table based on this real experience — remove or revise anything that didn't actually hold up in practice.

followUps.label: Add the output-destination column
followUps.prompt: Add an 'Output Destination' column to the table if it's missing — where does each task's finished output actually go (a shared drive, a specific Slack channel, direct email to a stakeholder, the PM tool)? Base it only on what I actually do, not a generic assumption.

followUps.label: Simplify into a quick-reference card
followUps.prompt: Condense this into a single-page quick-reference card: just task name, cadence, and the one most important verification action per task, dropping the fuller detail into a separate linked appendix instead.

pm-a1-pm-operating-system-templates-work.walkthrough:
Grace has been a PM for three years and has, without ever writing it down, developed her own working system: a specific prompt for meeting notes, a status report format she trusts, a way of building work breakdowns. None of it is documented, and when a new PM joined her team last month, she realized she'd been explaining the same habits verbally, differently, three separate times.

She opens Claude and writes out her real notes on five recurring tasks: meeting notes (Claude, verified against raw notes before sending), weekly status reports (Claude, verified that the status line matches the actual content), work breakdowns at kickoff (Claude with the clarifying-questions approach, verified against team capacity), risk registers (Claude, verified that mitigations are specific rather than "monitor closely"), and difficult stakeholder messages (Claude, but she admits she doesn't have a defined verification step — she just rereads it once).

The assembled table comes back with five rows, cadence and tool columns filled in from her notes, and four rows with the exact verification actions she described. The fifth row, for difficult stakeholder messages, is flagged clearly: "needs a defined verification step — not specified," rather than the AI inventing a plausible-sounding one on her behalf.

Grace decides on a real verification step for that row — check that no invented date or commitment appears — and adds it herself. She runs the assembled system for one full sprint, and it holds up except that her risk-register cadence turns out to be monthly in practice, not per-project as she'd first written, so she corrects it. She saves the final one-pager to the team drive and walks the new PM through it in one fifteen-minute session instead of three scattered conversations. Total build time: about 25 minutes, plus one sprint of real-world testing before calling it final.
